Whether such contexts shape life chances, or merely assemble people whose trajectories were already fixed, has structured the field's methodological quarrels for a generation. Christopher Jencks and Susan Mayer's 1990 review argued that existing neighborhood studies could not separate contextual influence from residential sorting, and Robert Sampson's book Great American City documented the persistence of neighborhood inequality in Chicago across several decades; a body of work incapable of distinguishing context from sorting cannot be squared with a documented multi-decade record of neighborhood inequality in one city. That unresolved impasse over separating context from sorting led directly to the adoption of within-family comparison as a remedy. Random assignment of that sort and purely observational inference are mutually exclusive: either the demonstration allocated units by lottery, or it relied entirely on observational comparisons of volunteer families with no random assignment, and exactly one of those two descriptions can hold of it. Those interim results became available only after the 1994 launch of the demonstration. The interim Moving to Opportunity evaluation documented improvements in adult mental health among movers.
